10. Comparability Over Time and Space

Observed data collection methods have been applied consistently over time and space to the extent possible and adjusted for proper consistency otherwise. As described in Section 9, NOAA employs a rigorous process to adjust for changes over time in station location, methods, or instrumentation—or to weed out stations that are too inconsistent to adjust.

GCMs inherently use consistent algorithms over time and space.

The observed and projected time series and maps cover the same spatial extent: the CONUS. Observed and projected series reflect the same indicator definition, although the former is naturally derived from station data while the latter is derived from a grid.

11. Data Limitations

Biases in measurements may be present as a result of changes over time in instrumentation, measuring procedures, and the exposure and location of the instruments. Where possible, data have been adjusted to account for changes in these variables. Uncertainties in observed precipitation data increase as one goes back in time, as there are fewer stations early in the record. However, these uncertainties are not sufficient to undermine the fundamental trends in the data. EPA’s U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator also includes data for Alaska, but Alaska could not be included in this pairing because the STAR-ESDM downscaling product is limited to the CONUS.

Future projections of any variable have inherent uncertainty, as described in Section 12 below. Precipitation is influenced by multiple factors, so it may be less direct to model than, say, surface air temperature.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. Error estimates are not readily available for U.S. or global precipitation, but Vose and Menne (2004) suggest that the station density in the U.S. climate network is sufficient to produce a robust spatial average.

Model outputs inevitably reflect model uncertainty. Each GCM represents aspects of, and processes within, the climate system differently. These differences will lead to differences in how the GCMs represent both present-day climate and how the climate responds to changes in greenhouse gases. For example, GCMs differ in climate sensitivity, defined as the increase in global temperature when carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubles relative to pre-industrial times. Even a single GCM will yield different results if presented with different initial conditions, as the chaotic processes within the model will lead to different timing of various modes of variability within the model (such as the El Niño cycle). The shaded bands in the graph for this pairing illustrate this type of uncertainty in the spread of models, as well as year-to-year variations due to internal variability within each model.

Interpreting projections also requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents four widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

The choice of downscaling approach introduces a source of uncertainty relating to the technique and data used in the downscaling model. However, this uncertainty is typically smaller than the uncertainty stemming from the spread in climate models and scenario uncertainty (e.g., Lafferty and Sriver, 2023; Wooten et al., 2017).

13. Sources of Variability

Annual precipitation anomalies naturally vary from location to location and from year to year as a result of normal variation in weather patterns, multi-year climate cycles such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation and Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and other factors. The construction of this pairing addresses variability in a few ways:

  • Presenting a long-term record (more than a century of observed data) and averaging consistently over time and space.
  • Using anomalies to provide a common frame of reference.
  • Using annual totals to reduce some of the “noise” inherent in daily measurements or monthly totals.
  • Smoothing GCM outputs with an 11-year moving average.
